name: Janai Purnima at Gosaikunda
when: Shrawan full moon, usually August (sometimes late July)
summary: On the full moon of Shrawan, thousands of Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims climb to Gosaikunda at 4,380 m to bathe in the sacred lake, renew the janai thread and receive the raksha doro, while jhankri shamans drum and dance through the night.
body: Janai Purnima is celebrated across Nepal on the full moon of the month of Shrawan. Brahmin and Chhetri men change the janai, the sacred cotton thread worn across the chest, after ritual bathing and prayers, and people of all castes receive a yellow or red raksha doro tied around the wrist by a priest for protection. In many homes it coincides with Raksha Bandhan, when sisters tie rakhi on their brothers' wrists. Families also eat kwati, a soup of mixed sprouted beans.

Gosaikunda hosts the largest mountain gathering of the day. Pilgrims believe that bathing in the lake created by Shiva's trident washes away sins, and many walk for two or three days from Dhunche through monsoon forest to reach the shore by the full-moon night. Jhankri, the traditional shamans of Tamang and other hill communities, arrive in white robes and feathered headdresses to drum, chant and dance around the lake until dawn. In Patan, a parallel mela is held at the Kumbheshwar temple pond, believed to be fed by Gosaikunda's water.

For visitors, the festival is an extraordinary sight but a demanding trip. It falls in the monsoon, so the trail is wet and leech-ridden, the road from Kathmandu can be blocked by landslides, and clouds often cover the mountains. Lodges at Chandanbari, Lauribina and the lake overflow, and many pilgrims sleep in tents or crowded halls. Going with an organised group that carries tents and food, and arriving a day or two before the full moon, makes the experience safer and far more comfortable.
tips: Leave Kathmandu at least three days before the full moon so you can acclimatise at Chandanbari and Lauribina.
Pack rain gear, leech socks, a warm down jacket and a dry change of clothes for after the holy dip.
Book transport and rooms or tents early; road and lodge capacity is stretched for the whole week.
Respect the jhankri rituals: watch from a distance, do not use flash and ask before photographing.
Consider a helicopter yatra on a day before or after the full moon if walking 5–6 hours a day is not possible.

faqs.q: When is Janai Purnima at Gosaikunda?
faqs.a: Janai Purnima falls on the full moon of the Nepali month of Shrawan, usually in August and occasionally in late July. Pilgrims arrive at Gosaikunda the day before and bathe at dawn and through the full-moon day. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many people visit Gosaikunda during Janai Purnima?
faqs.a: Thousands of pilgrims, Nepali and Indian, climb to the lake over the festival days, making it the busiest time of year by far. Lodges are full, trails are crowded and food supplies run short. Organised groups bring tents and supplies, and arriving a day early helps avoid the peak.

faqs.q: Is it safe to trek to Gosaikunda in the monsoon?
faqs.a: It can be done safely with care. Expect rain, slippery stone steps, leeches and possible landslides on the road and lower trail. Altitude is still a factor at 4,380 m. Go with a guide, allow acclimatisation nights, carry rain gear and check road and weather conditions before leaving Kathmandu.

faqs.q: Can I fly to Gosaikunda for Janai Purnima?
faqs.a: Helicopter yatras do operate around the festival, weather permitting, but monsoon clouds often delay or cancel flights and landing space is limited when crowds are large. Flying the day before or after the full moon is usually more reliable. Prices rise in festival week; check current status before you book.

name: Sonam Lhosar, the Tamang New Year
when: Magh Shukla Pratipada, January or February
summary: Sonam Lhosar is the New Year of the Tamang people, celebrated in January or February with family feasts, monastery prayers, Tamang Selo songs and damphu drum dances. In villages such as Gatlang it is the biggest celebration of the year and a public holiday across Nepal.
body: Sonam Lhosar marks the start of the new year in the Tamang calendar and falls on the first day of the bright half of the month of Magh, in January or February. It is observed by the Tamang community and some other Himalayan groups, and is a national public holiday in Nepal. Each year is linked to one of twelve animals of the Tibetan zodiac, and people greet each other with Lhosar wishes and white khada scarves.

In the villages of Rasuwa, including Gatlang, Thuman and Briddim on the Tamang Heritage Trail, preparations start days in advance. Houses are cleaned and decorated, new prayer flags are raised and families prepare special foods such as khapse fried biscuits, sel roti and meat dishes, with local millet beer. On the day, people visit the gompa for prayers led by lamas, then gather with relatives. In the evenings groups sing Tamang Selo, the community's folk songs, and dance to the round, tambourine-like damphu drum.

In Kathmandu, large public celebrations take place at Tundikhel and around Boudhanath, with cultural programmes, stalls and Tamang communities in traditional dress. For trekkers, being in a Tamang village during Lhosar is a rare chance to see the community at its most festive, though it falls in the coldest part of winter. Nights in Gatlang drop near freezing, but skies are often clear and the trail quiet.
tips: Plan a Tamang Heritage Trail trek around the Lhosar date for village celebrations, and book homestays ahead.
Bring a white khada scarf to offer when greeting hosts or visiting the gompa.
Accept food and drink offered by hosts graciously; it is fine to decline alcohol politely.
Pack warm layers, as Lhosar falls in the coldest weeks of the year in the hills.
If staying in Kathmandu, visit Tundikhel or Boudhanath for the public celebrations.

faqs.a: Sonam Lhosar falls on Magh Shukla Pratipada, the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Magh, usually between late January and mid-February. It is a national public holiday in Nepal. Dates follow the lunar calendar and change every year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How is Tamang Lhosar different from Gyalpo Lhosar?
faqs.a: Sonam Lhosar is the New Year of the Tamang community and comes first, in Magh. Gyalpo Lhosar, celebrated by Sherpa and Tibetan communities, falls about a month later, in February or March. Tamu Lhosar of the Gurung community falls around late December. Each follows its own calendar and customs.

faqs.q: Can tourists join Lhosar celebrations in Gatlang?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors staying in homestays are usually welcomed to share food, watch the dances and visit the gompa with their hosts. Dress warmly and modestly, ask before photographing, and follow your hosts' lead at religious rituals. A small gift or contribution to the community fund is appreciated.

faqs.q: What food is eaten during Sonam Lhosar?
faqs.a: Families prepare khapse fried biscuits, sel roti, meat dishes such as pork or mutton, and local millet beer and spirits. Vegetarian guests will still find plenty of rice, vegetables and sweets. Food is shared with relatives and neighbours throughout the festival days.
